walkthroughs.body_html:
Materials — a core area of GCSE Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Materials brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Materials.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

An atom of Mg loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺. Its number of protons is:
How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.

mcqs.q: At which electrode are positive ions reduced during electrolysis?
options: Positive ions are reduced at the anode because that's where positive things go.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
At the cathode (the negative electrode) — positive ions gain electrons there.
Positive ions are oxidised at the cathode by losing protons.

mcqs.q: Why are most transition metal complex ions coloured?
options: Transition metal ions are coloured because they have a half-full d-subshell which naturally absorbs light.
Ligands split the d-orbitals into two energy levels; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them (d-d transitions), and the complementary colour is transmitted.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Transition metals are coloured because their nuclei emit photons in the visible range.
